title: SLSA v1 Build track — the requirements a repository DECLARES, as evaluable rules
description:
GT-665. The last of the four standards GT-600 named. SLSA is a different shape from ISO/IEC 5055 and is built differently: ISO/IEC 5055 names 138 structural CWEs that only a code parser can decide, so it ships as an adapter over an external analyser (GT-662/GT-663). Most of the SLSA Build track is a property of the BUILD and of how the producer DECLARES it — who builds, from what, whether provenance is generated, whether the platform signs it — and a workflow file answers those directly. So these are NATIVE rules with a handler behind them, and the half that a filesystem genuinely cannot decide is named in `notEvaluableHere` rather than guessed at.

The requirement names below are taken from the specification, read on 2026-08-09 rather than recalled: https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.0/levels, https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.0/requirements, https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.0/provenance, https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.2/build-track-basics. This repository's declared target is Build L3 against v1.2 (reference/core/control-center/security/supply-chain-posture.md §2.1); v1.2's addition is the Source track, and the Build track levels L0–L3 it publishes are the same L0–L3 v1.0 specifies, so the Build-track requirement vocabulary is quoted from the v1.0 requirements page that v1.2 carries forward.

standard.name: SLSA
standard.edition: v1.0 Build track (levels as published in v1.2)
standard.title: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts — Build track

notEvaluableHere.why: A native rule handler is given a filesystem. It is NOT given the package registry, a Sigstore client or the build platform's control plane — and most of what separates Build L2 from Build L3 is a property of the PLATFORM, not of anything a repository can write down. Authoring a rule for those would return a verdict about a control nobody checked, which is worse than returning no rule. They are named here so their absence reads as a declared boundary rather than as coverage.
notEvaluableHere.consequence: A green verdict from this pack means the repository's DECLARED build satisfies the file-decidable half of Build L1 and Build L2. It is NOT an assertion that any published artifact reached a SLSA level: no level has been independently verified against these artifacts, which §2.3 of the mapping document already records. This pack is non-blocking for exactly that reason.

requirements.why: "All of the provenance's contents MUST be generated by the build platform's trusted control plane" and the signing key must be inaccessible to user-defined build steps. Both are properties of the platform's implementation. No file in a repository can decide either, and a repository cannot make itself compliant by declaring anything.

Ephemeral, mutually non-influencing build environments with cache-poisoning prevention. Also a platform property. GitHub's documented route to it is a reusable workflow, and item 3 of the mapping document records that this repository does not use one — but 'calls a reusable workflow' is GitHub's guidance, not the specification's predicate, so it is NOT authored as a SLSA rule.

requirements.id: Producer — Choose an appropriate build platform
requirements.why: "The producer MUST select a build platform that is capable of reaching their desired SLSA Build Level." That is a judgement about the platform's own attestation of itself, not a repository artifact.

`https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1` is served by the REGISTRY, not declared by the tree — `npm publish --provenance` mints it implicitly and nothing in this repository names the string. Verified live on 2026-08-09 instead: `npm view @beyondnet/evolith-cli@1.2.2 --json` returns `dist.attestations.provenance.predicateType: "https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1"`. A rule asserting it from files would be asserting the absence of evidence.

Whether a published version carries an attestation, and whether its signature verifies, is a question for the registry and Sigstore. A consumer answers it with `npm audit signatures`; a filesystem cannot. Item 6 of the mapping document — that provenance is asserted for `latest` only, with no per-version inventory — stays open for the same reason.

requirements.id: Hermetic and reproducible builds, and dependency pinning
requirements.why: NOT CLAIMED, and deliberately so. Hermetic builds were SLSA v0.1's L4 and the v1.0 release notes record that they were DEFERRED to a future version along with the source and common requirements; dependency completeness likewise belongs to a future Dependencies track. So pinning a GitHub Action by commit SHA rather than by a moving tag is an OpenSSF Scorecard check (Pinned-Dependencies) and NOT a SLSA Build-track requirement. This repository would fail such a rule — 47 `actions/checkout@v7` and 41 `actions/setup-node@v7` resolve to whatever the tag points at, against 4 SHA-pinned uses — and the rule is still not authored here, because putting a real defect under the wrong standard's name is how a compliance claim stops meaning anything.

notEvaluableHere.severityNote: Every rule is `MUST` with `blocking: false`, following the pairing GT-662 recorded for ISO/IEC 5055 and for the same two reasons. MUST is what makes GT-569 emit an ADVISORY when a rule does not run — without it a repository whose rules were all skipped gets `passed` over zero evaluated rules, the exact false assurance this corpus keeps finding. `blocking: false` is what stops that advisory from failing a build over a level this pack never claimed to verify: the pack reads the DECLARED build, and the levels themselves are unverified against the artifacts by the mapping document's own admission. A tenant that wants these to block sets it in its own overlay, which is the choice the Core proposes rather than makes.

rules.title: Build L1 — EVERY publishing path generates provenance, not just the main one
rules.description: SLSA Build L1 requires that "the build process MUST generate provenance that unambiguously identifies the output package by cryptographic digest", and the Producer requirement is that provenance is distributed to consumers "preferably using a convention determined by the package ecosystem". For npm that convention is a registry attestation, and it is produced by `npm publish --provenance` in a job the platform can identify. The rule is EVERY, not SOME, and that word is the whole rule: a second publishing path without the flag distributes an artifact with no provenance while the repository's main path looks compliant. This one is written from a real asymmetry — `ci-cd.yml` published `src/sdk/cli` a second time with `--tag beta` and no provenance until GT-570 retired that job on 2026-07-27 — and from item 5 of the mapping document, which states in as many words that nothing verifies attestation presence automatically and a future release could silently drop `--provenance` with no check noticing. This is that check.
rules.rationale: A publish step is the only place a repository can generate provenance, and it is one flag away from not doing it. `npm publish --dry-run` is excluded: it publishes nothing, so it distributes nothing and cannot be held to a distribution requirement.
rules.validationQuery: Native handler: every non-dry-run `npm publish` step under .github/workflows carries `--provenance`. No publishing step at all ⇒ the Build track has no subject and the rule does not apply.

rules.title: Build L1 — the artifact is built by the run whose provenance describes it
rules.description: SLSA's Producer requirement for Build L1 is to "build their artifact in a consistent manner such that verifiers can form expectations about the build process", and Build L1's platform requirement is provenance that "unambiguously identifies the output package". A workflow that publishes without building first ships whatever happened to be in `dist/` when the checkout was packed, and the provenance then describes a run that did not produce the bytes it attests. That failure is invisible in a workflow file and looks exactly like compliance. It is not hypothetical here: `npm-release.yml` carries a comment saying that seven of the eight packages have no `prepublishOnly`, so `npm publish` would otherwise ship whatever is in `dist/` — the workflow builds every workspace precisely to stop that.
rules.rationale: Scope is stated rather than implied: the handler compares TEXT ORDER inside one workflow file — a build step appearing before the first publish step — and does not resolve the `needs:` job graph. A build in a job that a publishing job depends on but that appears later in the file would be read as absent. That is a false RED and the rule says so instead of hiding it; the alternative is a YAML parser inside the domain layer, which crosses the boundary the architecture lint defends.
rules.validationQuery: Native handler: in every workflow with a non-dry-run publish step, a build invocation (`npm run build`, `tsc`, `nest build`, `npm run prepublishOnly`) appears before the first publish step.

rules.title: Build L2 — the PUBLISHING job can mint the identity that signs the provenance
rules.description: SLSA Build L2 adds "Provenance is Authentic": the provenance must be signed, and the verifier must be able to establish that it came from the build platform's control plane. On GitHub Actions publishing to npm, that signature is minted through an OIDC exchange, and the exchange is impossible unless the job carries `id-token: write`. A `--provenance` flag on a job without that permission does not produce weaker provenance — it produces none, and the publish fails or ships bare. The permission is therefore the file-decidable half of authenticity. The question is asked of the JOB that publishes, not of the file: a workflow that grants `id-token: write` to some other job has granted it to something that does not publish, and a file-level match would certify that. GT-600 shipped exactly that class of defect twice in the SSDF pack (`PS.3.2` accepted any upload step anywhere, `RV.1.2` accepted any workflow mentioning CodeQL), so this one reads the job block.
rules.rationale: A workflow-level `permissions:` block grants to every job and satisfies the rule; a job-level block satisfies it for that job alone. Both shapes are live in this repository — `npm-release.yml` declares it at workflow level, `sdk-cli-release.yml` inside `publish-npm` — and both are fixtures.
rules.validationQuery: Native handler: for each job containing a non-dry-run publish step, `id-token: write` appears either in the workflow-level permissions header or inside that job's own block.

rules.title: Build L2 — nothing offers a way to publish from a workstation
rules.description: SLSA Build L2's isolation requirement reads: "All build steps ran using a hosted build platform on shared or dedicated infrastructure, not on an individual's workstation." A repository cannot prove where a past publish ran, but it CAN be checked for whether it still offers a route that bypasses CI: a package manifest whose scripts invoke `npm publish` is a workstation publish path by construction, and one that exists gets used. This repository is the case study — the mapping document records that everything except `src/sdk/cli` was published by hand from a developer machine until `npm-release.yml` existed, which is why versions before it carry no attestation and never will.
rules.rationale: Two things this rule does NOT claim. It does not treat `runs-on: self-hosted` as a violation: the specification says "shared or dedicated infrastructure", and dedicated infrastructure is explicitly allowed, so a self-hosted runner is a decision about the platform and not a defect a repository declares. And its scope is the package MANIFESTS reachable from the workspace declaration — not arbitrary shell scripts, which a filesystem handler cannot enumerate without guessing at what a human runs. A `npm publish` inside a script the manifests do not name is outside what this rule sees, and saying so is the difference between a boundary and a blind spot.
rules.validationQuery: Native handler: no `package.json` script in the root manifest or in a declared workspace invokes a non-dry-run `npm publish`.
